Case studies

Seven case studies, each one traced from the question that started it to what it actually produced and found — and to how far you can check the result from where you are sitting.

Viewing as All Water Climate & DRR Sustainable AI ESG & CSRD

Everything

Seven case studies, joined by one question: what does the data actually say, and who is it for? Water first, then climate risk, now the footprint of the tools themselves, and how to report it.

  • climatematch-pipeline — climate extremes for West Africa, public code, in the Climate & DRR view (Research outputs)

Water resources & WASH From the drill bit to the river mouth

I started underground. A geology degree, then electrical-resistivity surveying to find water in hard rock, then drilling crews delivering 164 water points across Sierra Leone. Later the same question at basin scale: what reaches the coast, and who put it there. The through-line is that water problems are rarely only hydraulic — the borehole that works is the one the community can maintain.

Best fit for: Roles in water resource management, WASH programming, hydrogeology, or utility planning — especially where field delivery and analysis have to meet.

  • 164 water points delivered — 100 wells rehabilitated, 50 boreholes, 14 solar-powered
  • 70% aquifer strike rate on survey-sited boreholes, from field records
  • 10,226 sub-basins modelled for river pollution export
  • MSc thesis proposing soft-path alternatives to hard water infrastructure

Climate adaptation & disaster risk Planning for the year the river wins

Disaster risk is a data problem before it is an engineering one — you cannot reduce what you cannot compare. At UNDRR that meant auditing Caribbean loss data and standardising the terminology behind it. In Wuppertal it meant asking a municipality what it would take to keep a suspended railway out of a flood, and turning climate projections into a roadmap somebody could act on.

Best fit for: Roles in climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction, resilience planning, or climate-risk analysis — particularly where frameworks like Sendai, CSRD or TCFD are in play.

  • 54 global hazard information systems documented for UNDRR
  • Caribbean disaster-loss data audited for the Sendai Framework Monitor
  • National risk-management factsheet for Trinidad and Tobago
  • Six-person flood-resilience consultancy for the Municipality of Wuppertal
  • climatematch-pipeline — climate extremes for West Africa, public code (Research outputs)

Sustainable AI & AI governance Every prompt has a footprint

The newest thread, and the one that made the rest make sense: the tools we now use to analyse environmental problems have environmental costs of their own, and almost nobody is measuring them. At the Digital Society School I am building the framework and the decision-support tooling for a finance ministry adopting generative AI — mapping Scope 2 electricity, Scope 3 hardware and data-centre water, in a reporting language the organisation already speaks.

Best fit for: Roles in sustainable AI, AI governance, green software, or ESG where digital footprint is in scope — and anywhere the job is to make an environmental claim survive scrutiny.

  • Sustainable-AI framework and prototype for the Dutch Ministry of Finance
  • EcoPrompt Coach — a public tool with a full evidence ledger behind every factor
  • Framework framed against CSRD/ESRS disclosure logic
  • This site: a first view of ~276 KB with its fonts, budgeted and enforced in CI

ESG & CSRD reporting The right number on the right disclosure line

A sustainability report doesn't want one number: it wants the right number on the right line, with its range and its source. GAIA, the open framework I wrote and maintain, is a method for doing that with an organisation's AI use: Scope 2 location- and market-based and never blended, Scope 3 for what it buys, water under ESRS E3, every figure a low, central and high value, and every output mapped to GRI, ESRS, IFRS S2, CDP and SBTi. Anatomy of a Prompt draws the same split for one query. The accounting underneath, Scope 1 to 3, materiality and transition planning, I worked through in the OnePointFive sustainability consulting accelerator. This is method and tooling; no client's assessment is claimed.

Best fit for: Roles in ESG and sustainability reporting, CSRD/ESRS readiness, GHG accounting or sustainability consulting — especially where an organisation's digital or AI footprint is in scope.

  • GAIA Framework 2.2: an open (MIT) specification, Excel workbook and web estimator
  • Outputs mapped to GRI 302/303/305, ESRS E1 and E3, IFRS S2, CDP and SBTi — a mapping, not an assurance
  • Anatomy of a Prompt: one query placed on the lines of a CSRD report
  • OnePointFive sustainability consulting accelerator, Cohort 7: Scope 1–3 accounting, materiality, transition planning

Every case study below is on this page in every view — a lens reorders and frames, it never hides. Each result says whether you can check it from outside, and how it is known.

2025 — present · Amsterdam, NL

Sustainable AI Framework

Making a finance ministry's AI adoption accountable for its footprint

Digital Society School, Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences · with Ministry of Finance (Ministerie van Financiën) · Researcher — Sustainable Artificial Intelligence

01 Problem

Generative AI is becoming government infrastructure — but every prompt has a footprint. How does a finance ministry adopt AI responsibly without greenwashing, and without grinding innovation to a halt?

02 Method four steps
  • Mapped the environmental footprint of generative AI end to end — Scope 2 electricity, Scope 3 hardware, and data-centre water.
  • Built a sustainability assessment framework for concrete AI use cases, framed against CSRD/ESRS disclosure logic so the output lands in a reporting language the ministry already speaks.
  • Prototyped decision-support tools with real users at both ends of the organisation: managers setting strategy, and employees writing prompts.
  • Aligned the framework against UN SDG 12 (responsible consumption and production) and SDG 13 (climate action).

03 Artifact

  • tool Public
    EcoPrompt Coach — this site's edition

    Energy, water and carbon per LLM query across named models and grids, with every emission factor's source, range and review date shown in an evidence ledger.

  • code Public
    EcoPrompt Coach — the maintained tool (promptcoach)

    Version 2 of the Digital Society School prototype: a JavaScript engine, web app and Chrome extension (unpacked, in no store), with its own method and newer models.

  • code Public
    Sustainable AI Prototypes

    Browser prototypes and a Chrome extension v1.0 from the November 2025 team project; its README lists my role as SCRUM Master & Integration Lead. Its success metrics are targets, not results.

  • framework Held by the client
    Sustainability assessment framework for AI use cases

    Developed inside a research partnership; not mine to publish unilaterally.

    Held by Digital Society School / Ministry of Finance.

04 Result

  • A working decision-support prototype, not a slide deck

    Checkable from outside The team's browser prototypes, a prompt coach and dashboard among them, are public on GitHub as Sustainable AI Prototypes, whose README records my role. This site's EcoPrompt Coach is a separate edition, with its own code.

  • Framework tested with users at both ends of the organisation

    Not checkable from outside Public research sessions and demo days in Amsterdam, with managers and day-to-day users. Qualitative — no completion or satisfaction metric was collected.

05 Findings & recommendations

  • Finding Between the most and least efficient model on the same task, the gap can exceed an order of magnitude, and few tools put it in front of the person typing the prompt.

    Basis The factor set behind the EcoPrompt Coach, adapted from Jegham et al. (2025), model by model in its evidence ledger.

  • Finding The framework came down to five design principles, among them "make the invisible visible" and a go/no-go checkpoint.

    Basis The printed cards in the photos below; the framework itself is not public.

  • Recommendation Before calling a bigger model, ask whether the demand itself can be smarter: the soft-path question from water, put to AI.

    Basis Field note 03, on the homepage.

Caveat This work is in progress and the outcome measures are qualitative. Any figure describing adoption or emissions avoided would be a guess, so none is given.

2025 — 2026

GAIA — Green AI Assessment

Method and tooling that put AI's footprint on a sustainability report's lines, uncertainty included

Open source (MIT licence) · Author and maintainer

01 Problem

An organisation that uses AI may have to report on it, and its sustainability report has no line called "AI". How do prompts become figures on the lines it has — energy, Scope 2 and 3, water — without more precision than the data allows?

02 Method three steps
  • Rebuilt the framework on published science in four modules, Ground, Assess, Interpret and Act: energy, carbon and water per request and per month, each a low, central and high value whose spread is set by the data's quality tier.
  • Reported Scope 2 location- and market-based side by side, never blended, and mapped each output to the disclosure line it fills: GRI 302, 303 and 305, ESRS E1 and E3, IFRS S2, CDP and SBTi.
  • Put one query on those lines on this site: Anatomy of a Prompt places the calculator's query on Scope 2, Scope 3 and ESRS E3.

03 Artifact

  • framework Public
    GAIA Framework — specification, Excel workbook and web estimator

    MIT-licensed. Workbook and estimator are generated from the same data tables, so they cannot drift apart.

  • tool Public
    GAIA web estimator

    One page, no external requests: model explorer, scenario comparison, portfolio inventory and per-lever savings, for workloads you type in.

  • figure Public
    Anatomy of a Prompt

    The calculator's query on a CSRD report's lines: electricity on Scope 2, cooling water on ESRS E3, embodied hardware on Scope 3 (drawn, not quantified).

04 Result

  • The workbook, the web estimator and the reference code give the same answers: 3,984 cross-engine checks pass

    Checkable from outside tests/test_engine.py, in the repository, runs them on the same cases and fails if any disagrees; its roadmap records 3,984 passing at version 2.2.0. An engineering fact, not a result for any organisation.

  • Each output mapped to the disclosure line it fills in GRI, ESRS E1 and E3, IFRS S2, CDP and SBTi

    Checkable from outside The table, data/alignment.csv, is in the repository and a sheet of the workbook since version 2.1.0. A mapping of outputs to line items: no assurance or certification is claimed.

05 Findings & recommendations

  • Finding Whose report AI's carbon lands on depends on who runs the model: its electricity is Scope 2 for the provider, or a team hosting its own; buying answers from a hosted model, as most teams do, it is the buyer's Scope 3, category 1.

    Basis Anatomy of a Prompt's boundary note, and FRAMEWORK.md, section 8, in the repository.

  • Finding One score hid more than it showed: GAIA 1.0 added watt-hours, litres and grams with invented weights. Version 2 has no composite: each use case's energy per request is graded against its task class's bands, with a frugality flag beside it.

    Basis DECISIONS.md and the 2.0.0 changelog entry, in the repository.

  • Recommendation Get real evidence in first: 117 of the 119 current models in GAIA's database are modelled, not measured, so measurements, provider disclosures and actual usage come next.

    Basis The repository's roadmap, section 0, at version 2.2.0.

Caveat Method and tooling, not a client result: nothing here is a real organisation's assessment. The tool sees only hypothetical workloads a user types in; it cannot read actual usage.

2023 — 2024 · Wageningen, NL

Coastal Water Pollution Dynamics

What drives river-borne pollution, and what Africa's coasts look like by mid-century

Wageningen University & Research · MSc thesis research

01 Problem

Rivers carry whatever we put in them straight to the sea. How do income, urbanisation and agriculture shape the export of multiple pollutants across the world's sub-basins — and what does that mean for Africa's coasts by mid-century?

02 Method four steps
  • Modelled river export of multiple pollutants with the MARINA-Multi model across 10,226 sub-basins worldwide.
  • Identified the socioeconomic drivers behind the resulting pollution patterns statistically.
  • Built qualitative future storylines for African coastal waters, including a deliberately pessimistic 'Dirty Delta' scenario.
  • Integrated climate-change scenarios into the projections.

03 Artifact

  • thesis On request
    MSc thesis — socioeconomic drivers of river export of multiple pollutants, and qualitative future storylines for African coastal water pollution

    Examined and defended at Wageningen University & Research. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

  • narrative On request
    Scenario storylines for African coastal waters

    Including the 'Dirty Delta' scenario. Part of the thesis.

04 Result

  • 10,226 sub-basins modelled

    Not checkable from outside The sub-basin count of the MARINA-Multi model configuration used — a property of the model domain, not an estimate.

  • Identified the socioeconomic factors that dominate coastal pollution export

    Not checkable from outside Statistical analysis of model output against socioeconomic drivers. The finding is in the thesis; effect sizes are not restated here because they cannot be checked without it.

  • Scenario storylines that turn model output into policy conversation

    Not checkable from outside Qualitative scenario method. Written to be argued with, not to be scored.

05 Findings & recommendations

  • Finding The thesis sets out which of income, urbanisation and agriculture dominate what rivers carry to the coast, and by how much; the effect sizes are not restated here, as they cannot be checked without it.

    Basis The thesis's regression of the model's output, on request.

  • Recommendation Write the storyline first and let it demand the numbers: model output rarely moves a policymaker, a story they can picture does.

    Basis Field note 02, on the homepage, on the "Dirty Delta" scenario.

Caveat A pessimistic scenario is a device for surfacing what people would rather not plan for. It is not a forecast, and is not presented as one.

2023 · Wuppertal, DE

Flood-Resilient Wuppertal

Keeping a city — and its suspended railway — out of the water next time

Wageningen University & Research — Academic Consultancy Training · with Municipality of Wuppertal · Interdisciplinary team of six

01 Problem

Wuppertal's iconic suspended railway glides above a river that flooded catastrophically in 2021. The municipality asked: how do we keep the city — and the Schwebebahn — out of the water next time?

02 Method four steps
  • Worked in a six-person interdisciplinary team across climate science, engineering and policy.
  • Assessed flood risk to the city and its transport infrastructure using historical records, climate projections and GIS.
  • Facilitated stakeholder workshops to map the social drivers of vulnerability, not just the hydraulic ones.
  • Translated the analysis into an implementation roadmap the municipality could act on.

03 Artifact

  • report Held by the client
    Consultancy report — 'Becoming a Boat: Towards a Flood-Resilient Wuppertal'

    Delivered to the client under the Academic Consultancy Training programme.

    Held by Municipality of Wuppertal / Wageningen University & Research.

  • tool Public
    Flood cross-section — interactive

    A schematic Wupper cross-section, below (it needs JavaScript): slide the river from a calm day to July 2021 and watch the clearance under the Schwebebahn's hanging cars shrink.

04 Result

  • A complete flood-risk management framework delivered to the municipality

    Not checkable from outside The deliverable of the consultancy: accepted and presented to municipal stakeholders. Held by the client.

  • Critical infrastructure vulnerabilities identified alongside cost-effective interventions

    Not checkable from outside GIS and climate-projection analysis, cross-checked in stakeholder workshops. Whether the recommendations were implemented is not something I can claim — that is the municipality's to report.

05 Findings & recommendations

  • Finding Flood vulnerability in Wuppertal is social as well as hydraulic: the workshops mapped land use, housing inequality and social cohesion among its drivers.

    Basis The stakeholder workshops, one of them in the photos below.

Jun 2023 — Oct 2023 · Bonn, DE

UN Disaster Risk Reduction — hazard data

You cannot reduce disaster risk with messy data

United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) · Climate Change Adaptation Intern

01 Problem

UNDRR needed clean, comparable hazard information to support the Sendai Framework — especially for small island states, where one storm can erase years of development.

02 Method four steps
  • Audited Caribbean disaster-loss data against external datasets for the Sendai Framework Monitor and the Losses & Damages Tracking System.
  • Documented global hazard information systems, expanding regional and hazard-type coverage.
  • Standardised disaster-reporting terminology across sources, so economic loss and damage meant the same thing in each.
  • Built a risk-management factsheet for Trinidad and Tobago.

03 Artifact

  • dataset Held by the client
    Inventory of 54 global hazard information systems

    Contributed to the organisation's internal databases.

    Held by UNDRR.

  • report Held by the client
    Risk-management factsheet — Trinidad and Tobago

    Produced for national policy use.

    Held by UNDRR.

04 Result

  • 54 global hazard information systems identified and documented

    Not checkable from outside A count of the systems catalogued during the internship, recorded in the deliverable. Countable, not estimated.

  • Regional and hazard-type coverage expanded by 25%

    Not checkable from outside Measured against the size of the organisation's existing catalogue at the start of the internship. The baseline is internal to UNDRR, so an outside reader cannot check it — which is why it is stated with its basis rather than on its own.

05 Findings & recommendations

  • Finding Disaster risk is a data problem before it is an engineering one: you cannot reduce what you cannot compare, so loss and damage had to mean the same in every source.

    Basis The audit and the terminology work in the method above; the records are UNDRR's.

Caveat Internship deliverables sit inside the organisation. The counts are real and were recorded; the baselines they are measured against are not public.

2020 — 2021 · Changsha, CN

Soft Path Water Management

What if the answer isn't more pipes?

Hunan University · MSc thesis research

01 Problem

Freetown keeps building bigger pipes, and keeps running dry. The uncomfortable question: what if the answer isn't more hard infrastructure at all?

02 Method four steps
  • Analysed Freetown's water-management challenges end to end, from supply through governance.
  • Developed soft-path alternatives: managing demand, capturing and reusing water close to where it is used, and community stewardship of the assets.
  • Evaluated feasibility specifically for resource-constrained settings, rather than assuming a European maintenance budget.
  • Packaged the result as an implementation framework other cities can reuse.

03 Artifact

  • thesis On request
    MSc thesis — 'Approach to soft path water management: thinking beyond cement, steel and pipes', Freetown as case study

    Defended at Hunan University, May 2021. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

04 Result

  • Successfully defended at Hunan University, May 2021

    Not checkable from outside Degree awarded — MSc Industrial Engineering, 2021. The certificate is the evidence, on request.

  • A community-centred alternative to pipe-and-pump thinking, scoped for fast-growing cities in the Global South

    Not checkable from outside The thesis's contribution, as examined. It is a proposed framework, not a deployed one — no city has implemented it, and no cost saving is claimed.

05 Findings & recommendations

  • Finding Bigger pipes have not closed Freetown's water gap: the city keeps building them, and keeps running dry.

    Basis The thesis's starting point and argument, as examined; on request.

  • Recommendation Manage demand, capture and reuse water close to where it is used, and give communities stewardship of the assets, judged against a resource-constrained city's means.

    Basis The framework the thesis proposes; no city has implemented it.

Caveat This is a proposal that passed examination, not an intervention that was built. The distinction matters and is kept.

2016 — 2017 · Freetown, SL

Groundwater Potential Mapping

De-risking the drill bit in hard rock

University of Sierra Leone · BSc dissertation, then applied in the field

01 Problem

The Freetown Complex is geologically stubborn — hard igneous rock where finding water is a gamble. Communities were paying for dry boreholes. The science needed to de-risk the drill bit.

02 Method four steps
  • Applied electrical-resistivity surveying to detect groundwater in hard rock.
  • Combined geological and hydrogeological data into GIS groundwater-potential maps.
  • Validated the predictions through field drilling campaigns — the only test that counts.
  • Produced siting recommendations for future boreholes.

03 Artifact

  • thesis On request
    BSc dissertation — 'Mapping groundwater potential in the Freetown Complex: a geophysical approach'

    First class honours, University of Sierra Leone. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

  • dataset On request
    Groundwater-potential maps for the Freetown Complex

    Produced during the dissertation and used in subsequent siting work.

  • code Public
    Groundwater Investigation Toolkit

    Python and browser code: field data in; figures, designs and .docx reports out. It dates from 2026, years after this work: a toolkit, not this project's deliverables. Its examples are partly illustrative.

  • tool Public
    Site the borehole — interactive resistivity profile

    A playable version of the reading the method depends on. Play it below (it needs JavaScript): read the resistivity curve, place the rig, drill, and set your strike rate beside the field records.

04 Result

  • 70% aquifer strike rate in subsequent drilling

    Not checkable from outside Successful strikes as a share of boreholes drilled on sites selected with the survey method, during the Team & Team International fieldwork. The site sets it beside roughly 30% for blind siting in the same geology, but no source for that baseline is recorded — so wherever the 30% appears it is labelled illustrative, not measured.

  • Method carried into the borehole siting that followed, part of 164 water points delivered across Sierra Leone

    Not checkable from outside The boreholes behind the 70% strike rate were sited with the survey method in the Team & Team International fieldwork. They are part of the 164 water points — 100 hand-dug wells rehabilitated, 50 boreholes constructed, 14 solar-powered boreholes, itemised and summing to 164 — but not all of them: a rehabilitated well needs no siting, and no survey siting is recorded for the other boreholes. The mapping informed siting; it is not the sole cause of the outcome.

05 Findings & recommendations

  • Finding In the Freetown Complex's hard rock, a low-resistivity dip is a lead, not an answer: it can mean water-bearing fractures, or clay.

    Basis The reading the survey method rests on, which the game below lets you try.

  • Recommendation Collect the data before the drill bit, not after: a wrong guess is a dry hole a community has paid for.

    Basis Field note 01, on the homepage.

Why it is laid out like this

The reasoning, and what the build checks

A portfolio that lists outcomes without saying how they were measured is asking to be taken on trust. Splitting each project into problem → method → artifact → result → findings makes the weak link visible: a strong method with an internal-only artifact is a different thing from a public tool anyone can run, and both from a number with no baseline behind it.

The content lives in content/projects.json. A test fails the build if a result loses its basis, a case study its findings, an artifact claims to be public without a working link, or a link points somewhere this repository has not already vouched for.
